title: Sworn by a star that sets on time.
subtitle: Why a setting star opens the surah
then: This was the first surah with a prostration, recited by the Prophet ﷺ publicly to the Quraysh. It opens with an oath. Mujahid said the star is the Pleiades as it sets at dawn. What the oath confirms comes next: {idea}your companion has not strayed.{/idea}
now: You check the sunrise time on your phone and it is right to the minute. The sky keeps its schedule while you are asleep. {idea}Order you never had to arrange.{/idea} That steady sky is the opening witness for what comes next.
old: The night sky is pretty, but it has nothing to say to me.
new: The sky keeps its order, and that order is called as a witness.
try: Step outside tonight for one minute and find one star. Let it remind you that the truth also keeps its path.

title: Your companion is not lost, and not crooked.
subtitle: Two different ways to go wrong, both denied
then: Allah calls the Prophet ﷺ {idea}your companion{/idea}: the man Quraysh had lived beside for forty years. Ibn Kathir explains the two denials. He is not {trap}lost like someone without knowledge{/trap}, and not {trap}crooked like someone who knows and turns away{/trap}.
now: Think of the friend you grew up with. You know how they act when nobody is watching. When a rumor about them goes round the group chat, you weigh it against years of seeing them up close. {idea}Long closeness is evidence.{/idea}
old: I judge a messenger by what people say about him today.
new: Those who knew him longest had already seen he was not lost or crooked.
try: Before you believe a rumor about someone today, ask what you have actually seen of them yourself.

title: He does not speak from what he wants.
subtitle: Words that do not come from the ego

row.title: Write!
sub: only truth comes out of me

then: Quraysh told Abdullah bin Amr to stop writing down the Prophet's ﷺ words, since {trap}he is human and speaks when angry{/trap}. He asked the Prophet ﷺ, who told him: {idea}Write. Only the truth comes out of me.{/idea}
now: You send a message in anger and spend the next day explaining what you really meant. Your words follow your mood. {idea}This verse describes a speaker whose words did not bend to his mood.{/idea} That is why his words can be trusted when yours, on a bad day, cannot.
old: Everyone's words are shaped by how they feel that day.
new: His message did not bend to his moods, so I can lean on it fully.
try: Next time you are angry, wait ten minutes before you send the message.

title: It is only revelation, delivered whole.
subtitle: No additions, no deletions
then: Ibn Kathir says the Prophet ﷺ {idea}conveyed what he was commanded, in its entirety, without additions or deletions{/idea}. When a man questioned one of his statements, he answered simply: I said what I said.
now: You forward a long message but quietly delete the line that makes you look bad. Or you add a bit to make it sound stronger. {trap}Most of us edit what we pass on.{/trap} The verse says this message reached you untouched.
old: Every message gets shaped a little by the one carrying it.
new: This one reached me exactly as it was sent.
try: Pass on one piece of news today exactly as you heard it, without adding or trimming.

title: His teacher was mighty in power.
subtitle: Jibril, the one who taught him
then: Ibn Kathir says the one {idea}mighty in power{/idea} is Jibril. Another surah calls him honorable, powerful, obeyed and trustworthy. {reward}A trustworthy angel brought it to a trustworthy messenger.{/reward}
now: You pick a surgeon, a lawyer, a tutor for your child, and you ask who trained them. A strong teacher makes you trust the student. {idea}This verse tells you who trained the Prophet ﷺ.{/idea}
old: He must have learned it from somewhere ordinary.
new: His teacher was Jibril, strong and trustworthy, carrying it from Allah.
try: Think of one good teacher you had and make a short dua for them today.

title: Strong and sound, he rose to his true form.
subtitle: The first time Jibril was seen as he is
then: Ibn Abbas reported that the Prophet ﷺ asked to see Jibril in his real form. {idea}A huge figure rose from the east and kept spreading.{/idea} Ibn Mas'ud reported he had six hundred wings, each filling a side of the horizon.
now: You see a mountain in photos for years, then one day you stand at its foot. The size stops you. {idea}Knowing about something and seeing it are different.{/idea} This verse is the moment the messenger saw his teacher as he really is.
old: The unseen world is probably small and vague.
new: What I cannot see is larger than anything I can picture.
try: Look at the widest sky you can find today and remember it is small next to what Allah created beyond it.

title: He stood on the highest horizon, where morning comes.
subtitle: The place the day begins
then: Ikrimah said the highest horizon is {idea}where the morning comes from{/idea}. Mujahid said the place of sunrise. Qatadah said, that from which the day comes. The Prophet ﷺ saw Jibril there, standing over the place where light begins.
now: You are driving early, and the eastern sky turns from grey to gold. Most mornings you barely notice. {idea}The same horizon once held the angel who carries revelation.{/idea} Dawn is not just weather.
old: Sunrise is just the start of a work day.
new: The horizon where day begins once held the carrier of revelation.
try: Watch the sky at dawn once this week, even through a window.

title: Then he came down and came close.
subtitle: The angel moves toward the messenger
then: Ibn Kathir says this describes Jibril {idea}descending to the Prophet ﷺ on earth{/idea} and drawing near. In the narration from Ibn Abbas, when the Prophet ﷺ fell unconscious at the sight, Jibril came down and revived him.
now: You think of guidance as something you must climb toward, alone, after you fix yourself. This verse shows the opposite movement. {reward}The message came down and came close.{/reward} It is already near you, on a shelf or in a phone app.
old: Guidance is far away and I have to reach it myself.
new: Guidance was brought down and brought close to me.
try: Open the Quran today, even for one verse, since it already came this close.

title: Two bow lengths away, or nearer.
subtitle: How close the angel came
then: Mujahid and Qatadah said this is the distance of two bows drawn to full length. Ibn Kathir explains that {idea}or nearer{/idea} confirms the distance and leaves no room to doubt it, like the verse on hearts as hard as stones {trap}or harder{/trap}.
now: Someone tells you about an event secondhand, and you ask, were you really there? How close were you? {idea}This verse answers that question exactly.{/idea} The witness was near enough to measure the distance.
old: A report about the unseen must be vague and distant.
new: The one who received it was close enough to measure the distance.
try: When you share something you heard today, say plainly how close you were to the source.

title: He revealed to His servant what He revealed.
subtitle: A message left unnamed, and a title kept
then: Ibn Kathir gives two meanings, both correct: Jibril conveyed what he conveyed, or Allah revealed through Jibril. Sa'id bin Jubayr said part of it was {reward}Did He not find you an orphan{/reward} and {reward}We raised high your fame{/reward}.
now: At the highest moment of his life, the Prophet ﷺ is called {idea}His servant{/idea}. Not leader, not genius. You spend energy building a title on a CV or a profile. Here the highest title is belonging to Allah.
old: Honor means a big title and people knowing my name.
new: The highest honor is to be called His servant.
try: In your next prayer, pause on the word abd in the tashahhud and feel what it means.

title: The heart did not lie about what it saw.
subtitle: Sight and heart agreed

row.title: true
sub: the heart did not deny it

then: Ibn Kathir records a discussion among the Companions on what he saw. A'ishah said {idea}it was Jibril{/idea}, seen twice in his true form. Ibn Abbas was reported saying he saw his Lord with his heart. Either way, the verse says the sight was true.
now: You saw something with your own eyes, and later people keep telling you that you imagined it. Slowly you start doubting yourself. {idea}This verse settles it for the Prophet ﷺ: what he saw was real.{/idea}
old: Maybe the whole thing was only in his head.
new: His heart and his sight agreed. What he saw was true.
try: Write down one clear moment when you felt Allah's help, so you do not let doubt erase it later.

title: Will you argue with him about what he saw?
subtitle: Arguing with an eyewitness
then: The people of Makkah argued with the Prophet ﷺ over what he described. {trap}They had seen nothing, yet they disputed.{/trap} The verse turns it into a question: {idea}will you argue with a man about what he saw with his own eyes?{/idea}
now: A nurse tells you what happened on the ward last night and you argue with her from your sofa. It sounds silly put that way. {trap}Yet we often argue hardest about things we never witnessed.{/trap}
old: My opinion is as good as his account.
new: Arguing with an eyewitness from a distance is not thinking. It is stubbornness.
try: In your next disagreement, ask first: was I there, or am I guessing?

title: He saw him a second time.
subtitle: The second sighting, on the Night Journey
then: A'ishah reported that the Prophet ﷺ told her {idea}it was Jibril{/idea}, seen only twice in his real form. Ibn Kathir says this second time was {idea}during the Night of Isra{/idea}, the night journey.
now: You notice something once and wonder if you imagined it. You see it again, exactly the same, and your doubt is gone. {idea}A second witness of the same thing settles the matter.{/idea}
old: One strange experience proves nothing.
new: He saw the same angel, in the same true form, a second time.
try: Recall two separate times a prayer of yours was answered. Let them steady you today.

title: At the Lote Tree where everything stops.
subtitle: The boundary of the seventh heaven
then: Ibn Mas'ud described Sidrat al-Muntaha as {idea}in the seventh heaven{/idea}. There everything that rises from the earth ends and is held, and everything that comes down from above ends and is held. The Prophet ﷺ saw Jibril there.
now: Your deeds, your duas, the quiet good you did on a Tuesday. You never see where they go. {reward}This verse names a place where what rises from the earth arrives.{/reward} Nothing you send up just vanishes.
old: My small prayers disappear into nothing.
new: What rises from the earth reaches a known place and is held there.
try: Make one sincere dua today and trust that it is going somewhere.

title: Right beside it, the Garden of Refuge.
subtitle: Paradise placed next to the boundary
then: The vision is located precisely: the Lote Tree, and {reward}near it the Garden of Abode{/reward}. The Prophet ﷺ was shown where Paradise lies. The listeners in Makkah were being told that the Garden is a real place, not a story.
now: You are tired of moving, of rent, of a hospital corridor, of never feeling settled. The word here is refuge, a place you come to rest. {reward}That home is real, and it has an address.{/reward}
old: Paradise is a nice idea, far and vague.
new: The Garden is a real place of refuge, shown and located.
try: When you feel unsettled today, say quietly: my real home is the Garden of Refuge.

title: Covered by what covered it.
subtitle: A sight too great to list
then: Ibn Kathir says angels, Allah's light and {reward}spectacular colors{/reward} covered the Tree. Ibn Mas'ud said golden butterflies. That night the Prophet ﷺ was given {reward}the five prayers{/reward}, the closing verses of al-Baqarah, and forgiveness of grave sins for those who do not associate partners with Allah.
now: You pray Maghrib in a rush between work and dinner. That prayer was a gift handed over at the highest place a human ever stood. {idea}The five prayers came from beside that Tree.{/idea}
old: The daily prayers are a routine to get through.
new: My five prayers are a gift brought back from the highest place.
try: Before your next prayer, take one breath and remember where it came from.

title: His sight did not wander or overreach.
subtitle: Discipline at the greatest moment
then: Ibn Abbas said his sight did not turn right or left. Ibn Kathir calls this {idea}a tremendous quality{/idea}: he did only what was commanded and {idea}did not ask beyond what he was given{/idea}, even surrounded by wonders.
now: You open your phone to answer one message and twenty minutes later you are deep in someone else's feed. {trap}Eyes that wander take the heart with them.{/trap} At the greatest sight ever shown, his eyes stayed where they were meant to be.
old: Looking around is harmless. My eyes go where they want.
new: A steady gaze is a form of obedience, even among wonders.
try: Open your phone today for one task, do it, and close it.

title: He saw some of his Lord's greatest signs.
subtitle: Signs that point to Allah's greatness
then: Ibn Kathir links this to the Night Journey verse: {idea}that We might show him of Our signs{/idea}. These were signs testifying to Allah's might and greatness. Some scholars took this verse to mean he saw signs, not Allah Himself.
now: A newborn's grip around your finger. A storm over the city. A scan on a doctor's screen. You saw a sign and moved on. {idea}A sign is meant to point past itself.{/idea}
old: Amazing things are just amazing things.
new: Every great sign is pointing me to its Lord.
try: Notice one thing today that amazes you and say SubhanAllah out loud.

title: Now look at al-Lat and al-Uzza.
subtitle: From the greatest signs to a stone and a tree
then: Right after the vision, the surah asks: have you considered these? Al-Lat was {trap}a white stone in Ta'if{/trap} with a house built around it. Al-Uzza was {trap}a tree at Nakhlah{/trap} revered by Quraysh. Ibn Jarir said both names were taken from Allah's names.
now: You would never bow to a stone. But you might check one app before you pray, or fear a boss's mood more than Allah. {trap}We all have things we quietly give too much weight to.{/trap} The question is for you too: have you considered them?
old: Idols are an old problem that has nothing to do with me.
new: Anything I give Allah's place to deserves a hard look.
try: Name one thing that pulls your attention before Allah does. Look at it honestly.

title: And Manat, the third one.
subtitle: Three famous idols, three tribes
then: Manat stood at Mushallal near Qudayd, between Makkah and Madinah. {trap}Aws, Khazraj and Khuza'ah revered it{/trap} and began their Hajj from beside it. Ibn Kathir says there were many idols in Arabia, but {idea}these three were named because they were the most famous{/idea}.
now: Every family has its sacred thing nobody questions: the way it has always been done, what the neighbors will say. {trap}The most famous habits are the hardest to look at.{/trap}
old: If everyone around me respects something, it must be fine.
new: Even the most famous thing can be just a name.
try: Pick one family habit you follow without thinking and ask whether it pleases Allah.

title: Sons for you, daughters for Him?
subtitle: They gave Allah what they disliked for themselves
then: The idolaters claimed the angels were Allah's daughters, while preferring sons for themselves. Ibn Kathir explains the question: {trap}do you choose female offspring for Allah and keep the males for yourselves?{/trap} Their own logic was turned back on them.
now: You keep the best for yourself and hand Allah the leftovers: the tired last prayer of the night, the coins at the bottom of your pocket. {trap}We give Him what we would not accept ourselves.{/trap}
old: Whatever I give Allah is fine, even if it is my leftovers.
new: If I would not accept it myself, why offer it to Him?
try: Give something today from what you like most, not what is left over.

title: That is a crooked division.
subtitle: Unfair even between people
then: Ibn Kathir explains: {trap}if you split things like this between yourselves and other people, it would be unjust{/trap}. How then can you make that split between yourselves and Allah? The word means unfair, crooked.
now: You notice instantly when a sibling gets the bigger share of an inheritance. Your sense of fairness is sharp when it is about you. {idea}This verse asks you to use that same sharpness about what you give Allah.{/idea}
old: I notice unfairness only when it is done to me.
new: The fairness I demand from others, I owe in what I give Allah.
try: Think of one place you expect more from others than you give. Even it out today.

title: Only names you and your fathers invented.
subtitle: Guesswork and desire, while guidance has arrived
then: Ibn Kathir says they had {trap}no proof except trust in their forefathers{/trap}, plus a desire to lead and to keep their fathers honored. Meanwhile {idea}guidance had already come to them{/idea} through the Messengers.
now: Someone asks why you do something, and the only answer you have is: that is how my family does it, or everyone in my circle thinks so. {trap}A name and a habit are not proof.{/trap}
old: Our ways are right because our elders handed them down.
new: A name without proof is only a name, however old it is.
try: Ask yourself why you hold one belief today, and look for its proof.

title: Does a person get whatever he wishes?
subtitle: Wishing is not the same as earning
then: Ibn Kathir says {trap}not everyone who claims to be guided is truly guided{/trap}, and not everyone gets what he wishes for himself. He cites the hadith: {idea}when one of you wishes, let him be careful what he wishes for{/idea}, for he does not know what of it will be written.
now: You tell yourself you will become a better person someday, you will pray properly after this busy season, after the wedding, after the exam. {trap}A wish is not a plan.{/trap}
old: I mean well, so it will work out for me.
new: Wishing for good is not the same as walking toward it.
try: Turn one good wish into one small step you take today.

title: Both lives belong to Allah.
subtitle: The last and the first, in one hand
then: After the question about wishes, the answer: {idea}all matters belong to Allah{/idea}, King of this world and the next. Ibn Kathir says whatever He wills occurs, and {idea}whatever He does not will never occurs{/idea}.
now: You plan your career, your house, your retirement, as if this life were yours to run and the next one far away. {idea}Both are in the same Hands.{/idea} The one who decides your payday decides your ending too.
old: This life is mine to run. The next one is far away.
new: This life and the next belong to the same Owner.
try: Add in sha Allah sincerely to one plan you make today.

title: Even angels intercede only with His permission.
subtitle: So what can a stone do?
then: The idolaters hoped their idols would intercede for them. Ibn Kathir reasons: {idea}if this is the case with angels who are close to Him{/idea}, how can anyone hope for the help of idols without His permission? He links it to the Throne Verse.
now: You look for the right contact, the cousin who knows someone, the person whose word will fix your problem. {trap}We trust connections.{/trap} Even the highest beings need Allah's leave. Go to Him first.
old: If I know the right person, my problem is solved.
new: No one can help me without Allah's leave, so I ask Him first.
try: Before you call anyone for help with a problem today, ask Allah first.

title: Not believing in the Hereafter, they named angels female.
subtitle: Careless claims grow where accountability is denied
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah admonishes the idolaters for {trap}calling the angels by female names and claiming they were Allah's daughters{/trap}. He cites another verse: did they witness their creation? {idea}Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned.{/idea}
now: When you think no one will ever check, you say things more loosely. A review you never verified. A claim about someone at work. {idea}Belief in a Day of questions makes your words careful.{/idea}
old: What I say about things I cannot see does not really matter.
new: Every claim I make will be recorded and asked about.
try: Before you state something as fact today, ask yourself: could I answer for this?

title: Guessing never takes the place of truth.
subtitle: No knowledge, only assumption
then: Ibn Kathir says {trap}conjecture is of no benefit and never takes the place of truth{/trap}. He quotes the Prophet ﷺ: {idea}Beware of suspicion, for suspicion is the most lying speech.{/idea}
now: Your colleague did not reply to your message, and in your head a whole story builds: they are angry, they dislike you, they are plotting. {trap}It is all a guess.{/trap} A guess, however detailed, is still not the truth.
old: I am pretty sure, so it is basically true.
new: A guess, however confident, is worth nothing against the truth.
try: Catch one assumption you make about someone today and ask them instead.

title: Turn from the one who wants only this world.
subtitle: When someone has turned their back on the Reminder
then: The Prophet ﷺ was told to {idea}withdraw from the one who turns away from the Reminder{/idea}. Ibn Kathir describes such a person as one {trap}whose aim and knowledge are concentrated on this life{/trap} alone.
now: You spend hours in comment threads arguing with someone who has no interest in listening. Your evening is gone, your heart is heavier. {idea}Some conversations are a signal to step back.{/idea}
old: I must win every argument about faith.
new: When someone has turned away, I can step back and guard my own heart.
try: Leave one pointless argument today, online or off, without a last word.

title: That is as far as their knowledge reaches.
subtitle: When this world is the whole syllabus
then: Ibn Kathir says seeking this life was {trap}the best knowledge they had acquired{/trap}. He mentions the supplication: {idea}O Allah, do not make this world our greatest concern, nor the limit of our knowledge.{/idea}
now: You know your phone plan, the best exchange rate, the price of every car you might buy. {trap}Can you say as much about what comes after?{/trap} The verse names a ceiling many of us live under.
old: Being well informed about this world is enough.
new: If this world is all I know, my knowledge has stopped too early.
try: Say the dua today: O Allah, do not make this world my greatest concern.

title: Everything is His, so every deed is answered.
subtitle: Ownership leads to recompense
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah {idea}created the creation in truth{/idea} and rules it with justice. He repays each by their deeds. Notice the difference: evil is met with what it did, but good is met with {reward}what is best{/reward}.
now: You helped your neighbor carry boxes and nobody thanked you. You snapped at your child and nobody saw. {idea}Nothing in the world is ownerless, so nothing is lost.{/idea} And the good is repaid with more than it was.
old: Most of what I do goes unnoticed and unanswered.
new: Allah owns everything, so every deed is answered, and good with the best.
try: Do one good deed today that nobody will see.

title: Vast forgiveness, so do not praise yourselves.
subtitle: Avoid the big sins, and stay humble
then: Ibn Kathir says the good-doers avoid major sins, and their {reward}minor faults are forgiven{/reward}. He knew you in the womb. The Prophet ﷺ changed a girl's name from Barrah, the pious one, saying {idea}do not claim purity for yourselves{/idea}.
now: Your profile says blessed and grateful. In your head you rank yourself against the cousin who stopped praying. {trap}Self-praise is quiet and easy.{/trap} The verse reminds you who knew you before your mother did.
old: Compared to others, I am doing pretty well.
new: He knew me in the womb. Only He knows who is truly good.
try: When you feel better than someone today, stop and ask Allah to forgive you both.

title: Have you seen the one who turned away?
subtitle: A portrait that begins with turning
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah here {trap}chastises those who turn away from His obedience{/trap}. He links it to another verse: he neither believed nor prayed, but denied and turned away. The next verses fill in the portrait.
now: You used to read Quran after Fajr. Then once a week. Then the app sits unopened on your phone. {trap}Turning away rarely feels like a decision.{/trap} The verse asks you to look at the person who turned, and check your own direction.
old: Turning away is something other people do, dramatically.
new: Turning away can happen quietly, and I should check my direction.
try: Pick up one good habit you let slip, and do it once today.

title: He gave a little, then stopped.
subtitle: Like diggers who hit a rock and quit
then: Ibn Abbas said: {trap}gave a little, then stopped giving{/trap}. Ikrimah and Sa'id gave a picture: people digging a well hit a rock, say {trap}we are finished{/trap}, and abandon the work.
now: You set up a monthly donation, then cancel it the first tight month. You started visiting your aunt, then stopped after one awkward visit. {idea}The first rock is where giving is tested.{/idea}
old: I gave once. That counts, even if I stopped.
new: The test is not the first gift, but carrying on past the first rock.
try: Restart one small act of giving you dropped, even at a smaller amount.

title: Does he see the unseen, that he fears poverty?
subtitle: Stinginess pretends to know the future
then: Ibn Kathir says he stopped giving {trap}for fear of poverty{/trap}, as if he knew the future. The Prophet ﷺ said: {reward}Spend, Bilal, and do not fear less provision from the Owner of the Throne.{/reward}
now: Payday comes, you see a request for help, and the thought arrives: what if I need this later? {trap}That thought acts as if it can see next month.{/trap} It cannot. The Provider can.
old: If I give now, I might not have enough later.
new: I cannot see the future, but I know Who replaces what I spend.
try: Give a small amount today before the what-if thought finishes.

title: Has he not heard what Musa's scriptures said?
subtitle: An old message, already delivered
then: The surah asks whether this man was never told {idea}what is in the scriptures of Musa{/idea}. Ibn Kathir says the verses that follow are what Allah revealed in the scriptures of Ibrahim and Musa. The message was not new.
now: You hear a hard truth about responsibility and want to wave it away as someone's opinion. {idea}Some truths have been repeated by every prophet.{/idea} When something is that old and that consistent, it deserves a pause.
old: This is just one more opinion I can ignore.
new: This truth was already in Musa's scriptures. It is not new.
try: Read the next few verses slowly, as words told to many prophets before.

title: And Ibrahim, who fulfilled everything.
subtitle: One word that sums up a life
then: Ibn Abbas said {idea}he delivered all that Allah ordered him to deliver{/idea}. Qatadah said he obeyed Allah and conveyed His message. Ibn Kathir links it to the trials Ibrahim completed, after which Allah made him {reward}a leader for mankind{/reward}.
now: You finish nine steps of a task and leave the last annoying one for later. Most people do. {idea}Ibrahim is remembered with one word: he finished.{/idea}
old: Doing most of what is asked is good enough.
new: Ibrahim is honored because he fulfilled all of it.
try: Finish one task today that you left at ninety percent.

title: No one carries another's load.
subtitle: Each soul carries its own
then: Ibn Kathir says {idea}every soul shall carry its own wrongs{/idea}, and no one else will carry them. He cites another verse: if one heavily laden calls another to help, {trap}nothing will be lifted, even by a close relative{/trap}.
now: You grew up blamed for your brother's mistakes, or you lean on your parents' piety to cover your own gaps. {idea}Neither is how the scales work.{/idea} You are not carrying their load, and they are not carrying yours.
old: I will be judged with my family, or because of them.
new: I carry only my own load, and no one can carry it for me.
try: Let go of guilt for one thing that was someone else's choice, not yours.

title: You have only what you strive for.
subtitle: Effort is the currency
then: Ibn Kathir says the soul {idea}only benefits from the good it earns for itself{/idea}. Even the three things that continue after death in the hadith, {reward}a righteous child, ongoing charity, beneficial knowledge{/reward}, are in reality the results of one's own efforts.
now: You are raising kids, teaching a younger colleague, planting a tree outside the building. {reward}Those efforts keep counting after you stop.{/reward} What you build now is what you will have.
old: What I get in the end is mostly luck or other people.
new: What I get is what I strove for, including what keeps going after me.
try: Teach someone one useful thing today.

title: Your effort will be seen.
subtitle: Nothing done is invisible

row.title: it will be shown
sub: by the Knower of the unseen

then: Ibn Kathir says this means {idea}on the Day of Resurrection{/idea}, citing: Do deeds, Allah will see your deeds, and His Messenger and the believers. Then you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the seen, {reward}who will tell you what you used to do{/reward}.
now: You stayed late to fix a mistake that was not yours. You cared for a parent for years and nobody at work knew. {reward}It will be seen.{/reward} Nothing done for Allah is invisible.
old: If no one sees my effort, it is wasted.
new: Every effort will be seen, even the ones no one noticed.
try: Do one hidden kindness today and keep it between you and Allah.

title: Then it is repaid in full.
subtitle: The fullest recompense
then: The sequence ends here. The effort is made, it is seen, and {reward}then it is repaid with the fullest recompense{/reward}. Ibn Kathir says Allah repays in the best manner, good for good and evil for evil.
now: Your payslip never matches the hours you really put in. Your parents never got repaid for what they gave you. {reward}This verse promises a payment that is complete.{/reward}
old: Life never pays me back for what I give.
new: Nothing is underpaid with Allah. It comes back in full.
try: Think of one effort that felt unrewarded and hand it over to Allah in a short dua.

title: To your Lord is the final end.
subtitle: Every road ends at the same place
then: Ibn Kathir says this is {idea}the return of everything on the Day of Resurrection{/idea}. Mu'adh bin Jabal stood among the tribe of Awd and said he was the Prophet's ﷺ envoy to them: {idea}know that the return is to Allah{/idea}, to Paradise or the Fire.
now: You map out a career path, a five-year plan, a retirement date. Every plan has a last line. {idea}This verse writes the true last line for all of them.{/idea}
old: My plans end where my life ends.
new: Every road I take ends with my Lord.
try: Look at one plan you are making and ask: how does this end with Allah?

title: He makes you laugh, and He makes you weep.
subtitle: Both your tears and your laughter come from Him
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah {idea}created in His creatures the ability to laugh or weep{/idea}, and the causes for each. Both opposites are His work. The listeners of Makkah are being shown a Lord who is present in their most ordinary moments.
now: Morning: a voice note from your child that makes you laugh out loud. Evening: a call from the hospital. {idea}Both moments come from the same Lord.{/idea} Neither is outside His care.
old: My good days are luck and my bad days are bad luck.
new: Both my laughter and my tears come from Him, so I can turn to Him in both.
try: The next time you laugh today, say Alhamdulillah. The next time you cry, say it too.

title: He causes death, and He gives life.
subtitle: The two doors only He opens
then: Ibn Kathir links this to another verse: {idea}He who created death and life{/idea}, to test which of you is best in deeds. The surah keeps listing what only Allah does, against the idols named earlier.
now: A maternity ward and an ICU on the same floor of the same hospital. You walk past both on the way to the lift. {idea}Every arrival and every departure there is His decision.{/idea}
old: Life and death are decided by medicine and luck.
new: Only He gives life and only He takes it, so my days are in His hand.
try: Visit or call someone who is ill today.

title: He created the pairs, male and female.
subtitle: Two kinds, both His design
then: Earlier the surah rejected the claim that angels were Allah's daughters. Now it states that {idea}He creates both male and female{/idea}. Ibn Kathir links it to another surah: was he not a drop, then a clot, then shaped, then made into two sexes?
now: You look at a scan on the screen, waiting to hear boy or girl. {idea}Neither choice is yours, and both are His creation.{/idea} The verse puts that moment back in His hands.
old: One kind of child is more of a blessing than the other.
new: Both male and female are His creation and His gift.
try: Thank Allah today, by name, for each child or sibling in your family.

title: From a tiny drop, a whole person.
subtitle: The humble beginning of everyone
then: Ibn Kathir cites the verse: {trap}does man think he will be left neglected?{/trap} Was he not a drop? Then a clot, then shaped. It ends: {idea}is He not able to give life to the dead?{/idea} The beginning argues for the return.
now: You hold a newborn in the hospital and cannot believe something this whole began so small. {idea}The same power is behind the promise of resurrection.{/idea} Your start is proof of your return.
old: Resurrection is too hard to believe.
new: If He made me from a drop, bringing me back is not hard for Him.
try: Look at your own hand for ten seconds and remember it began as a drop.

title: Upon Him is the second creation.
subtitle: He made you once. He will make you again.
then: Ibn Kathir explains: {idea}just as He first originated creation, He is able to bring it back{/idea}, resurrecting it for the Day of Judgement. The answer to doubt about the return is the first creation itself.
now: You rebuild an app you once wrote and it takes a fraction of the time, because you made it before. {idea}Remaking is never harder for the one who made it.{/idea}
old: Once I am dust, that is the end of me.
new: The One who made me once has promised to make me again.
try: Say tonight before sleep: in Your name I die and I live.

title: He gives wealth, and He gives contentment.
subtitle: Two gifts: having, and being satisfied
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah gives wealth and lets it remain, so people can benefit from it. Mujahid said aghna is {reward}He gives wealth{/reward}. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid also said aqna means {reward}He gave contentment{/reward}.
now: Payday arrives, and two days later you feel just as short as before. Someone else earns half and sleeps fine. {reward}Wealth and contentment are two different gifts, and both are His.{/reward}
old: If I earn more, I will finally feel enough.
new: Wealth and contentment are separate gifts. I can ask for both.
try: In your dua today, ask Allah for contentment with what you have, by name.

title: He is the Lord of Sirius.
subtitle: The star they worshipped has a Lord
then: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said ash-Shi'ra is {idea}the bright star, Sirius{/idea}, which {trap}a group of Arabs used to worship{/trap}. The surah names it to say: even the brightest thing in your sky has a Lord.
now: A celebrity, a bright career, a big name on a stage. Some things shine so hard that people start treating them as more than human. {idea}Brightness is still created.{/idea} It has a Lord.
old: Some people and things are so impressive they deserve awe.
new: Even the brightest thing has a Lord. The awe belongs to Him.
try: When someone dazzles you today, say quietly: their Lord is greater.

title: He destroyed the former people of Ad.
subtitle: The strongest nation, gone
then: Ad were the people of Hud. Ibn Kathir says they were {trap}among the strongest and fiercest people{/trap}, and the most rebellious against Allah and His messenger. He links it to Iram of the pillars, and the wind sent on them for seven nights and eight days.
now: You feel safe because of what you have built: the job title, the savings, the strong body at the gym. {idea}Strength is a gift, not a shield against Allah.{/idea} Use it for Him.
old: If I am strong and secure enough, nothing can touch me.
new: Strength did not save Ad. Only turning to Allah keeps me safe.
try: Use one of your strengths today to help someone weaker.

title: And Thamud, none of them left.
subtitle: A whole people, no remnant
then: Ibn Kathir says this {trap}declares that He destroyed them all and spared none{/trap}. The surah lists the ruined peoples one after another, so the warning builds.
now: You read about a company that collapsed overnight, every job gone. You assume you would have seen it coming. {idea}The verse asks: what are you ignoring right now?{/idea}
old: Stories of ruined nations are history, not a message to me.
new: These stories are warnings for how I live today.
try: Name one warning sign in your own life you keep ignoring, and take one step about it.

title: Nuh's people before them were worse still.
subtitle: The longest warning, the hardest refusal
then: The people of Nuh came {idea}before Ad and Thamud{/idea}. Ibn Kathir says they were {trap}more unjust in disobeying Allah than those who came after them{/trap}. The surah moves backward through history to its first great refusal.
now: Someone keeps reminding you, kindly, for years: pray, call your mother, stop that habit. The longer you refuse, the easier refusing gets. {trap}Long refusal hardens.{/trap}
old: I have heard this reminder a hundred times. It does not move me now.
new: A long refusal is more serious, not less. I can still turn back.
try: Take one reminder you keep brushing off and act on it today.

title: The overturned towns, brought down.
subtitle: The cities of Lut's people
then: Ibn Kathir says these are {trap}the cities to which Prophet Lut was sent{/trap}. Allah turned their cities upside down over them. Like the other nations in this list, they had been warned by a prophet first.
now: You keep telling yourself a habit is harmless because everyone around you does it. {idea}Normal around you is not the same as right.{/idea} The verse invites a look at your own life, not your neighbor's.
old: If everyone in my circle does it, it cannot be that bad.
new: A warning ignored by a whole town is still a warning.
try: Look at one habit your circle treats as normal and ask honestly if Allah is pleased with it.

title: Covered by what covered them.
subtitle: Left unnamed, so it weighs more
then: Ibn Kathir says what covered them is like {trap}the stones sent on them{/trap}, citing: how evil was the rain of those who had been warned. The same phrase appeared earlier for the Lote Tree, which was covered with {reward}light and colors{/reward}.
now: Two people hear the same reminder on the same Friday. One goes home softer, one goes home annoyed. {idea}The same words can cover you with light or leave you exposed.{/idea} The difference is how you receive them.
old: Warnings are for people much worse than me.
new: The same message can lift me or condemn me, depending on how I receive it.
try: Take one reminder you hear this week and act on it within a day.

title: Which of your Lord's favors will you doubt?
subtitle: After the whole list, the question
then: Qatadah explained it as: {idea}which of Allah's favors for you, O man, do you doubt?{/idea} Ibn Jarir preferred this meaning. It closes the long list of what Allah does: laughter, tears, life, death, wealth, and the lessons of past peoples.
now: You scroll past a hundred blessings a day: hot water, a working phone, a friend who texts back. {trap}Then one thing goes wrong and you wonder if He cares.{/trap} The question is put to you.
old: I am not sure Allah has really been good to me.
new: The list of His favors is longer than my doubts.
try: Write down five favors from today before you sleep.

title: A warner, like the warners before.
subtitle: Not a new thing among the messengers
then: Ibn Kathir says the Prophet ﷺ was sent {idea}just like the warners of old{/idea}, citing: I am not a new thing among the messengers. The Prophet ﷺ described himself as {idea}the naked warner{/idea}, one who rushes to warn his people so fast he does not stop to dress.
now: Your friend sees smoke from your kitchen and runs in shouting, without shoes. You do not call that rude. {idea}A real warner is someone who loves you enough to hurry.{/idea}
old: Warnings in religion are just meant to scare me.
new: A warner hurries because he cares what happens to me.
try: Thank someone today who once warned you about something for your own good.

title: The near event has come near.
subtitle: The Day of Resurrection draws closer
then: Ibn Kathir says this is the {idea}Day of Resurrection, drawn nearer{/idea}, like the next surah's opening, the Hour has drawn near. He cites the Prophet's ﷺ warning about small sins: {trap}people each bring one stick until they have enough fire to bake bread{/trap}.
now: One skipped prayer. One small lie on a form. One unkind joke in the group chat. {trap}Each feels like a single stick.{/trap} The Day is coming closer while the pile grows.
old: There is plenty of time, and my sins are small.
new: The Day is near, and small sins add up like sticks on a fire.
try: Pick one small sin you repeat and drop it for today.

title: No one but Allah can lift it.
subtitle: Nobody can stop it or say when
then: Ibn Kathir says {idea}no one besides Allah can prevent it from coming{/idea}, nor does anyone know when it will come except Him. The warner hurries to tell people about it so that it does not catch them unprepared.
now: You cannot stop an exam date, a due date, a court date. You can only prepare. {idea}The Day is the same: not in your control, but your readiness is.{/idea}
old: If I cannot control it, why think about it?
new: I cannot stop the Day, but I can be ready for it.
try: Do one thing today you would want done if the Day came tomorrow.

title: Are you surprised by this message?
subtitle: Wonder that is really doubt
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah admonishes the idolaters because they {trap}hear the Quran, yet turn away from it in heedless play{/trap}. Their wondering was {trap}doubting that it is true{/trap}.
now: Someone shares a verse in the family chat and you react with a raised eyebrow, half amused, half dismissive. {trap}Surprise can be a polite way of not listening.{/trap}
old: Some of what the Quran says is just surprising, not serious.
new: My surprise should turn into reflection, not dismissal.
try: Take one verse that surprised you and read its tafsir this week.

title: You laugh, and you do not weep.
subtitle: The wrong response to the right words
then: Ibn Kathir says they laughed {trap}in jest and mockery{/trap}, and did not weep {reward}as those who believe in it weep{/reward}. He cites the believers who fall on their faces weeping, and it increases their humility. Earlier, the surah said He makes people laugh and weep.
now: You hear a heavy reminder in a talk and someone near you cracks a joke. You laugh too. {trap}Laughter can be a way to escape a feeling we should stay with.{/trap}
old: Making light of serious things is just my personality.
new: Some words deserve tears, and laughing them off is a loss.
try: Listen to one recitation today without your phone, and let it reach you.

title: While you amuse yourselves and look away.
subtitle: Distraction in place of listening
then: Ibn Abbas said samidun means {trap}singing{/trap}, from a Yemeni usage: sing for us. In another report he said it means {trap}turning away{/trap}, and Mujahid and Ikrimah said the same. They filled the air with noise rather than hear.
now: Silence makes you uneasy, so a podcast plays in the car, music in the kitchen, a video while you eat. {trap}There is never a quiet moment for anything to reach you.{/trap}
old: Background noise is harmless. It helps me relax.
new: Constant noise can be a way of turning away.
try: Spend five minutes in silence today with nothing playing.

title: So prostrate to Allah and worship Him.
subtitle: The verse that brought a whole gathering down
then: Ibn Abbas reported that when the Prophet ﷺ recited An-Najm and prostrated, {idea}those present prostrated with him{/idea}. Al-Muttalib bin Abi Wada'ah refused that day. After he became Muslim, {reward}he never heard this surah to its end without prostrating{/reward}.
now: You hear the call to prayer during a meeting, or a sajdah verse in a recitation, and you hesitate because people might watch. {idea}The whole surah has been building to this one movement.{/idea} It is never too late to make up a missed one.
old: I will bow down when the moment is more convenient.
new: After all these signs, the right answer is to fall down before Him.
try: Make one long, unhurried sujood today and stay in it a little longer than usual.
